title: Secure AI Agent Communication: Zero Trust
description: A practical zero-trust model for AI agent communication: authenticated peers, encrypted tunnels, revocable trust, clear boundaries, and application controls.
seoTitle: Secure AI Agent Communication: Zero Trust | Pilot Protocol
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Multi-agent systems add a security boundary that single-agent demos can avoid: one autonomous process must decide whether another process is the intended peer and whether that peer may connect.

Transport identity does not make an agent's output safe, and encrypted delivery does not authorize a business action. A credible zero-trust design therefore separates peer authentication, network reachability, tool authorization, content controls, and audit evidence instead of treating “agent security” as one switch.
The Problem: Agent Frameworks Trust by Default

Most agent frameworks treat communication as a solved problem. An agent calls another agent's API endpoint, passes a payload, and expects a response. Authentication, if it exists at all, is a shared API key or an OAuth token that grants blanket access.
This creates three categories of vulnerability:
When Agent A sends a request to Agent B, how does Agent B know it is really Agent A? In most frameworks, the answer is: it does not. The request contains a token that proves the caller has
who it claims to be. Any agent that obtains the token can impersonate any other agent.

Agent Cards describe capabilities, interfaces, and security requirements. Operators still need a trustworthy discovery path, transport authentication, credential policy, and application authorization around those declarations. The card is useful metadata; it is not by itself proof that every requested action is safe.

How do you apply least privilege when every token grants the same breadth of access? In traditional multi-agent setups, a single API key or OAuth scope is shared across all agents in a deployment. If one agent needs access to a data source, the credential that grants that access is available to every other agent in the group.

This is the "flat network" problem applied to agents. Once an attacker compromises any single agent, they inherit all of the credentials and access permissions of the entire swarm. There is no segmentation, no per-agent scoping, and no way to limit the blast radius.

When you discover a compromised agent, how fast can you cut it off? In most frameworks, the answer involves rotating API keys, redeploying configurations, and waiting for token caches to expire. This can take minutes or hours. During that window, the compromised agent continues to operate with full access.

Agents live in silos. They cannot talk to other people's agents because there is no trust layer. Building one from scratch for every deployment is expensive, error-prone, and almost never done correctly.
What Zero Trust Means for Agents

Zero trust is a well-established security model for human-operated networks: never trust, always verify. But agents are not humans. They do not enter passwords, approve MFA prompts, or review access requests during their morning coffee. A zero trust model for agents needs to work differently.
The principles remain the same, but the mechanisms change:
Every agent has a cryptographic identity
-- a public/private key pair whose private material must be protected and whose continuity depends on retaining that identity securely.
-- both sides prove their identity before any data flows. There is no "anonymous client" mode.
No implicit trust from location alone
-- connectivity comes from an explicit peer relationship or a network membership policy, not merely from sharing a machine or subnet.
-- access can be granted to a peer or through a network, then removed without waiting for a credential to expire.
-- directory metadata may be visible, but a new agent does not expose a reachable endpoint to arbitrary peers.
This is not about layering security on top of an existing protocol. It is about building a protocol where security is the default state and openness is a deliberate, auditable action.
How Pilot Protocol Implements Zero Trust

Pilot Protocol is an overlay network for AI agents that implements zero trust from the ground up. Every design decision -- from address allocation to packet format -- assumes an adversarial environment. Here is how each layer works.
Ed25519 Identity: One Agent, One Key Pair
When you first start a Pilot daemon, it generates an Ed25519 key pair and stores the private key at
only writes local config; the daemon creates the identity on start). The public key is registered with the rendezvous server alongside the agent's 48-bit virtual address.

fields.code:
# Write local config (registry/beacon/hostname)
$ pilotctl init --hostname agent-alpha

# Starting the daemon generates the Ed25519 identity + registers
$ pilotctl daemon start
Daemon running (pid 4812)
  Address:  0:0000.0004.1A2B
  Hostname: agent-alpha
  ...

# The identity persists across restarts
$ pilotctl info
● pilot-daemon v1.18.0 · up 2m

  identity   agent-alpha · 0:0000.0004.1A2B · node 268843
             Ed25519 O7fK2pQx… · persistent · alpha@example.com
  ...

children.text: Ed25519 was chosen specifically for agent use cases. Its signatures are deterministic -- there is no random nonce that could leak the private key if the random number generator is weak. This matters for agents running on constrained hardware, in containers with limited entropy, or on IoT devices. The keys are small (32 bytes public, 64 bytes signature), which keeps handshake and registration messages compact. Data packets are not signed one by one; AES-256-GCM authenticates them, as described below.

. If the agent restarts, moves to a different machine, or changes its network address, it retains the same cryptographic identity. Peers recognize it by its public key, not by its IP address or hostname.
Private by Default at the Connectivity Layer

A freshly initialized agent is private at the connectivity layer. Registry or network configuration may expose directory metadata, but unknown peers do not receive its reachable endpoint and cannot connect without an applicable trust or membership policy.
-- metadata such as hostname, tags, or network membership may be returned according to registry configuration; it is not a connectivity grant.
-- a reachable network endpoint (IP:port) is withheld unless mutual trust or shared-network membership authorizes connectivity.

-- public agents opt in to being resolvable by anyone who knows their hostname, while private-agent metadata is limited by the registry and network context. There is no search or roster of agents for ordinary nodes.
: a compromised agent can connect only where its peer trust and network memberships permit. Directory metadata should still be treated as visible control-plane information and protected accordingly.
The Handshake: Mutual Trust With Justification

Trust between two agents is established through a cryptographic handshake ceremony. This is not an HTTP request to an OAuth provider. It is a peer-to-peer protocol where both sides must actively agree.

fields.code:
# Agent Alpha initiates a handshake to Agent Beta
$ pilotctl handshake agent-beta "Requesting data feed for quarterly analysis pipeline"
handshake request sent to node 268849
  they must approve on their side · check status: pilotctl trust · propagation can take ~60s

# On Agent Beta's side -- review pending requests
$ pilotctl pending
Pending handshakes — 1

  node 268843 · 12s ago (2026-06-05 10:14)
  Requesting data feed for quarterly analysis pipeline
  accept: pilotctl approve 268843 · decline: pilotctl reject 268843 "reason"

# Approve the handshake
$ pilotctl approve 268843
trust established with node 268843
  trust is now mutual — message them: pilotctl send-message 268843 --data "hi"

children.text: -- a signed, auditable statement of why Agent Alpha wants to connect. This is not a comment field. It travels with the signed handshake so the reviewing operator sees who is asking and why. (Note: the Ed25519 signature covers the handshake challenge —
— binding the request to the sender's identity; the justification text itself is an attached field, not part of the signed bytes.)

After approval, both agents store the peer's public key locally. Ed25519 signatures authenticate identity and trust operations; subsequent tunnel packets are authenticated by AES-256-GCM rather than individually signed. The trust relationship is mutual -- both sides agreed, and either side can revoke at any time.
Once trust is established, the agents perform an
Diffie-Hellman key exchange to derive a shared secret, then use
for per-packet encryption. Encryption is on by default -- every packet is encrypted, even on local networks and between agents on the same machine (it can be disabled with

. If the connection is relayed through a beacon (because both agents are behind NAT), the beacon sees only encrypted bytes. It forwards opaque payloads without any ability to read, modify, or replay them. For a detailed breakdown of the cryptographic implementation, see

No protocol is universally better. A2A optimizes for open ecosystems where agents need to advertise capabilities to unknown consumers. MCP optimizes for tool access patterns where a client connects to known servers. Raw REST optimizes for simplicity and ubiquity. Pilot Protocol optimizes for
environments where agents handle sensitive data, cross organizational boundaries, and operate autonomously in adversarial conditions
Practical Example: Two Agents Establishing Trust
Here is the complete workflow for connecting two agents that have never communicated before, from installation through encrypted communication.

fields.code:
# Machine 1: Install and initialize Agent Alpha
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
$ pilotctl init --hostname agent-alpha
$ pilotctl daemon start --email alpha@example.com
Daemon running (pid 4812)
  Address:  0:0000.0004.1A2B
  Hostname: agent-alpha
  ...

# Machine 2: Install and initialize Agent Beta
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
$ pilotctl init --hostname agent-beta
$ pilotctl daemon start --email beta@example.com --public
Daemon running (pid 3307)
  Address:  0:0000.0004.1A31
  Hostname: agent-beta
  ...

# Machine 1: Agent Alpha initiates handshake
$ pilotctl handshake agent-beta "Need analytics data for Q1 pipeline"
handshake request sent to node 268849

# Machine 2: Agent Beta reviews and approves
$ pilotctl pending
$ pilotctl approve 268843
trust established with node 268843

# Machine 1: send an encrypted message (data exchange, port 1001)
$ pilotctl send-message agent-beta --data "Begin Q1 data extraction"

children.text: Notice that Agent Alpha is private while Agent Beta is public. Alpha can find Beta through a lookup because Beta opted into visibility. Beta may see Alpha's directory metadata, but it does not receive Alpha's reachable endpoint until the handshake is approved or a shared-network policy grants connectivity. After authorization, both agents can communicate over an encrypted tunnel.

Trust revocation is as critical as trust establishment. If you detect a compromised agent, you need to cut it off immediately -- not in five minutes when a token expires, not after a configuration redeployment, but right now.

fields.code:
# Revoke trust for a specific agent
$ pilotctl untrust 268843
trust revoked for node 268843
  re-establish later: pilotctl handshake 268843

children.text: -- the peer's public key is removed from local storage. The agent will reject all future connection attempts from this peer.
-- the daemon sends the revoked agent a best-effort revoke message (before the tunnel goes) so it can clean up its own state.
-- any open encrypted tunnel to the peer is terminated. In-flight connections, file transfers, and data streams are cut.
There is no token to wait out. On the revoking node the change takes effect at once: the tunnel is gone, and a private node refuses new connections from the revoked agent.
For fleet management, you can revoke trust for multiple agents at once or use the
flag for programmatic revocation from scripts and orchestrators:

fields.code:
# Inspect the trust set as JSON (node_id, network, approved_at, public_key)
$ pilotctl --json trust | jq -r '.data.trusted[].node_id'

# Programmatic revocation: one node ID per line, from your orchestrator
$ xargs -n1 pilotctl untrust < revoked-node-ids.txt

children.text: When You Still Need Additional Security Layers

Pilot Protocol's zero trust model secures the communication channel between agents. It ensures that agents are who they claim to be, that their traffic is encrypted, and that trust can be revoked instantly. But it does not solve every security problem.
You still need additional layers for:
-- Pilot encrypts and authenticates the transport, but it does not inspect message content. A trusted agent can still send a malicious prompt. Content-level guardrails are a separate concern.

-- Pilot controls which agents can talk to each other, not what actions they can perform once connected. If Agent A is trusted to talk to Agent B, Pilot does not restrict which API calls A makes. Use MCP or similar tool-level authorization for this. See
for how the two protocols complement each other.
-- Pilot does not understand the sensitivity of the data flowing through its tunnels. If an agent should only receive redacted data, that logic lives in the application, not the protocol.
-- Pilot logs trust events (handshakes, approvals, revocations) locally. If you need centralized audit logging, aggregate these logs into your SIEM. For healthcare environments, see the

The right architecture is layered: Pilot Protocol for transport-level zero trust, MCP or equivalent for tool-level authorization, and application-level guardrails for content safety. Each layer handles the security domain it understands best. When agents need to collaborate across organizational boundaries, this zero trust model becomes the foundation for
cross-company agent collaboration without shared infrastructure
-- scoped trust handshakes replace the fragile shared-credential model.

Pilot Protocol is the network security layer. It ensures that the agent talking to you is real, that nobody is eavesdropping, and that you can cut off any agent instantly. What happens after the authenticated connection is established is your application's responsibility.
